claims.text: Structural stability during catalytic operation at 773–1173 K is primarily governed by entropy of mixing.
Entropy of mixing influences phase segregation.
Entropy of mixing influences defect formation.
Adjusting constituent-element ratios changes the nanoparticles' entropy of mixing.
Phase stability mediates the structural response of the nanoparticles.
Defect density mediates the structural response of the nanoparticles.
Higher entropy of mixing produces a more homogeneous elemental distribution.
A more homogeneous elemental distribution reduces phase segregation.
Reduced phase segregation enhances high-temperature structural stability.
Higher-entropy nanoparticles will exhibit lower structural-degradation rates than lower-entropy nanoparticles under otherwise identical high-temperature catalytic conditions.
Higher-entropy nanoparticles will exhibit less phase segregation than lower-entropy nanoparticles under otherwise identical high-temperature catalytic conditions.
Lower-entropy nanoparticles will undergo significant structural degradation under the test conditions.
Lower-entropy nanoparticles will undergo significant phase segregation under the test conditions.
The proposed relationship may depend on the identities and interactions of the constituent elements.
The hypothesis may not apply to other nanoparticle classes or temperature regimes.
Higher entropy of mixing should improve catalytic performance relative to lower entropy of mixing.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome concerns structural degradation and phase segregation, but the falsification rule additionally requires improved catalytic performance. Thus, unchanged catalytic performance could formally falsify the hypothesis even when its stated structural prediction is confirmed.
